topic: View and Identify Processes to Monitor System Activity
prompt: List every process on the system in full format, showing UID, PID, PPID and the command.
explanation: -e selects every process and -f gives the full-format listing. Without options, ps shows only the processes tied to the current terminal.

topic: View and Identify Processes to Monitor System Activity
prompt: In ps output, what does a question mark (?) in the TTY column indicate?
options: The process has no controlling terminal — it is a daemon
The terminal could not be determined
The process is running on the graphical console
explanation: pts means a pseudo terminal, tty a physical one, Console the graphical console, and ? no controlling terminal at all — the signature of a background daemon.

topic: View and Identify Processes to Monitor System Activity
prompt: Which commands quickly return just the PID of a named process? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: pidof and pgrep both take a process name and return its PID; used without options they produce identical results. ps -C lists full process lines for a command name rather than bare PIDs.

topic: View and Identify Processes to Monitor System Activity
prompt: Which file system do ps and similar tools read to obtain process information?
explanation: The procfs virtual file system mounted at /proc exposes the kernel's live view of every process. It is created in memory at boot and destroyed at shutdown.

topic: View and Identify Processes to Monitor System Activity
prompt: Which tool shows continuously updated, real-time CPU and memory usage per process?
explanation: top refreshes live and is the natural way to spot CPU- or memory-intensive processes. Its columns include PR (priority), NI (niceness), %CPU and %MEM. Press q to quit, f to choose fields, F to pick the sort field.

topic: Inspect Process States and Understand How Execution Priority is Determined
prompt: What is a zombie (defunct) process?
options: A process that has finished but whose entry remains until the parent reads its exit status
A process stuck waiting on hardware I/O
A process running with the lowest possible priority
explanation: The five basic states are running/runnable (R), interruptible sleep (S), uninterruptible sleep (D), stopped (T) and zombie (Z). Uninterruptible sleep is the one that cannot be killed even with signal 9.

topic: Inspect Process States and Understand How Execution Priority is Determined
prompt: A process is stuck in state D and will not die even with `kill -9`. What does that state mean?
options: Uninterruptible sleep — it is waiting on hardware I/O and ignores signals
Defunct — the parent has not reaped it
Stopped — it needs SIGCONT to resume
Running — the scheduler has not preempted it
explanation: A process in uninterruptible sleep is blocked in a kernel I/O operation and cannot be interrupted by any signal. It often points to a storage hardware or driver problem.

topic: Adjust Process Niceness to Influence CPU Scheduling
prompt: What is the range of niceness values, and which end is the most favourable?
explanation: There are 40 values from -20 (most favourable, highest priority) to +19 (least favourable). Most processes start at the default niceness of 0, which corresponds to priority 80.

topic: Adjust Process Niceness to Influence CPU Scheduling
prompt: A normal user tries to launch a program with a niceness of -10 and is refused. Why?
options: Normal users may only raise niceness (lower priority); root is needed to lower it
The nice command requires the program to be in /usr/local/bin
explanation: Unprivileged users can only make their processes nicer to others. Increasing priority — moving niceness toward -20 — requires root, so the command needs sudo.

topic: Adjust Process Niceness to Influence CPU Scheduling
prompt: Launch the top program at a niceness of +2, which is lower priority than the default.
explanation: nice -n sets the starting niceness. The resulting process shows priority 82 and NI 2 in ps -l output. Use renice to change the niceness of an already-running process.

topic: Terminate, Pause, and Restart Programs with Signals
prompt: Which signal does kill or pkill send when you do not name one, and what does it do?
options: 15 (SIGTERM) — asks the process to stop in an orderly fashion
1 (SIGHUP) — makes the process re-read its configuration
explanation: SIGTERM is the default and lets the process clean up before exiting. Always try it first; SIGKILL is a last resort because it gives the process no chance to close files, risking data loss.

topic: Terminate, Pause, and Restart Programs with Signals
prompt: Match the control signals. Which pairings are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: 1 = SIGHUP, which makes a daemon re-read its configuration without restarting
explanation: 15 is SIGTERM, the soft termination signal; 9 is SIGKILL. SIGCONT (18) resumes a stopped process, like the bg command. kill -l lists all 64 signals.

topic: Terminate, Pause, and Restart Programs with Signals
prompt: Forcefully terminate every running process named crond by name, using signal 9.
explanation: pkill and killall act on process names, while kill needs PIDs. Ordinary users may only signal their own processes; root may signal any.

topic: Run Commands in the Future without Manual Intervention
prompt: Which daemons handle one-time and recurring scheduled jobs respectively?
options: atd for one-time, crond for recurring
crond for one-time, atd for recurring
anacron for one-time, crond for recurring
explanation: Neither daemon needs restarting after you add or change a job. crond skips jobs missed while the system was down; atd will attempt a missed at job when the system comes back up.

topic: Control Which Users can Schedule Tasks
prompt: /etc/cron.allow does not exist and /etc/cron.deny exists but is empty. Who may schedule cron jobs?
explanation: This is the default state, which grants everyone access. If neither file exists, no one but root may schedule. An allow file that exists but is empty permits no users, and its existence always overrides the deny file.

topic: Control Which Users can Schedule Tasks
prompt: Which statements about the at/cron access files are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: They hold one username per line
root is always permitted regardless of their contents
An existing allow file overrides the deny file
The four files are at.allow, at.deny, cron.allow and cron.deny
They must list UIDs rather than usernames
explanation: All four live in /etc and share the same one-username-per-line syntax. root's access is unaffected by whether it appears in them.

topic: Schedule and Manage One-Time Jobs
prompt: Which commands list or remove pending at jobs? (Select all that apply.)
options: atrm removes one by job ID
at -d removes one by job ID
explanation: atq and at -l are equivalent, as are atrm and at -d. Submitted jobs are spooled as files under /var/spool/at.

topic: Schedule and Manage One-Time Jobs
prompt: Which directory holds spooled at jobs, and which log records their execution?
explanation: at jobs spool to /var/spool/at and user crontabs to /var/spool/cron, but both services log every invocation to /var/log/cron. Reading that log requires root.

topic: Describe the Crontab Syntax to Automate Routine Tasks
prompt: What is the order of the five schedule fields in a crontab entry?
options: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week
hour, minute, day of week, day of month, month
day of week, month, day of month, hour, minute
minute, hour, month, day of month, day of week
explanation: Minute 0–59, hour 0–23, day of month 1–31, month 1–12 (or jan–dec), day of week 0–7 (0 and 7 both mean Sunday). Field 6 is the command to run.

topic: Describe the Crontab Syntax to Automate Routine Tasks
prompt: What does `*/5` in the minute field of a crontab entry mean?
options: Five minutes after the hour, once a day
explanation: The forward slash introduces a step value, so */5 fires every fifth minute and 0-59/4 every fourth. Step values work the same way in the hour, day, month and weekday fields.

topic: Schedule and Manage Recurring Jobs
prompt: Open your own crontab for editing.
explanation: -e edits, -l lists and -r removes your crontab. -u <user> targets another user's crontab, which requires the right privileges. The file opens in vim by default.

topic: Schedule and Manage Recurring Jobs
prompt: Where is user1's personal crontab file stored?
explanation: Each user's crontab is a file named after them in /var/spool/cron. The other two locations crond reads — /etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d — may only be modified by root.
